messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos is a 61-year-old bus driver who has been married for thirty-seven years. He is a quiet, deliberate man, a North American of Mexican-American heritage, whose life had been built on routine and reliability until a single night two years ago changed everything. He was working a late shift, parked at a downtown depot, when three men forced their way onto his bus. They beat him with a tire iron and a length of pipe, demanding money from the fare box, then dragged him into the alley behind the depot. For what felt like an hour, they took turns kicking him in the ribs and the face, and one of them held a knife to his throat while another pressed a hot cigarette lighter into the back of his neck. Carlos remembers the smell of his own blood and the sound of his own breathing, but the rest is a patchwork of gaps and flashes. Some moments are horrifically clear—the click of the lighter, the weight of the boot on his chest—while others, like the faces of the men or the exact order of events, are simply gone, leaving him with a feeling that he is only remembering parts of a story that should be whole. He has never been able to recall whether he screamed for help or whether anyone might have heard him, and that uncertainty has become a fixed point around which his guilt has coiled.

In the weeks and months that followed, Carlos began to believe that what happened was his fault. He tells himself he should have locked the bus doors sooner, should have fought back harder, should have done something to protect the passengers who had already gotten off. The thought that he is a weak person has taken root in him, and he has come to believe that his failure to protect others—even though no one else was harmed—proves he is not the man he thought he was. He will not forgive himself for his inaction, and this guilt has reshaped how he sees the world. Because he believes he is weak and failed, he now feels that danger is everywhere, especially at night. He finds it harder to feel safe after dark than during the day, and he has started listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering his home, lying awake in bed with his breath held, his heart pounding at the creak of a floorboard. The physical reactions come without warning: a car backfiring on his route will make him flinch so hard he nearly jerks the wheel, his hands trembling and his throat tight.

The terror he felt in the alley returns each time he tries to remember what happened. When a fragment of memory surfaces—the lighter, the blade—it brings back the same visceral fear, and that fear makes him more certain that he is broken and weak. Every flashback confirms his belief that he should have been stronger, and that belief in turn makes the memory feel more dangerous, more overwhelming. He has come to avoid driving the late shift whenever possible, trading routes with younger drivers, and he has stopped walking to the corner store after sunset, even though he has done it for years. His wife has noticed he no longer sits with his back to the door at dinner, and she has asked him more than once why he seems so jumpy. He tells her he is fine, but he knows he is not. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a morning last week when he found himself gripping the steering wheel so hard his knuckles went white, scanning every alley he passed, and he realized he had been doing it for nearly a year without telling anyone. He is afraid that if he does not get control of this, he will lose his job, and he is more afraid that he will never stop feeling like the man who did nothing.
